newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac reaffirms France wants Poland in EU in 2000.
newsitem.headline: Chirac reaffirms France wants Poland in EU in 2000.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac reaffirmed support on Monday for Poland to join the European Union in 2000 and for the former communist state to enter NATO.

Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski, playing down security concerns after four Polish protesters threw eggs at him during a two-day visit to Paris, praised Chirac's ideas as "promising and realistic" for Poland.
The European Commission reckons that EU enlargement to eastern Europe is unlikely before 2002.

"France has adopted a completely clear position in favour of Polish membership of the European Union and NATO," Chirac told reporters after talks with the former communist turned social democrat lasting about 90 minutes.

Chirac said that NATO would issue invitations for the first former Communist countries to join at a summit in Madrid on July 8. France wants Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Romania to be in the first wave of new alliance members.
Referring to the European Union, Chirac said: "If you want what I believe, it's that Poland will be a member in the year 2000. I said it in Warsaw, I am convinced that this will be the reality."
Chirac visited Warsaw last September and expressed hopes for Polish membership at the millennium. In the past year, he has also set the same target for the Czech Republic and Hungary to join.
"In any case, France will be at Poland's side in its course towards membership and will support it," Chirac said.
Chirac also proposed setting up a working group of officials from the French and Polish presidencies and representatives of foreign affairs and defence ministries to follow up the EU talks.

Neither man mentioned the attack on Sunday in which four Polish rightists threw eggs towards Kwasniewski outside a Paris theatre, which irked the Warsaw government over French security measures. Kwasniewski was not hit.
A French source said Chirac asked Kwasniewski about the attack at the start of their meeting. "The Polish president said it was not serious...they didn't discuss it for long," the source said.
In Warsaw, government spokeswoman Aleksandra Jakubowska took a harder line, saying "judging from the information we have, not everything was done to ensure proper security for the president."

"If eggs could reach (the president), so could...stones, if not hand grenades," she said. And private Radio Zet quoted Kwasniewski's spokesman as saying Poland was mulling a diplomatic note to France.

French officials said that Franco-Polish trade had expanded by 47 percent in 1996, making France Poland's fifth biggest trading partner. It was the fifth largest source of foreign investment in Poland last year.
